notice: Original synthetic excerpts, not compiled Android applications or observed runtime traces. Only the Notes Boundary project is buildable source; do not infer a successful dynamic test.

cases.title: Exported boundaries and ownership
questions: Which manifest and source evidence identifies the external caller boundary?
Why is exported=true alone not a vulnerability, and what control is missing in this excerpt?
How would a second controlled app and two mock accounts falsify the disclosure hypothesis?
feedback: An exported receiver with no guarding permission accepts external intents; intent extras supply untrusted id. The final merged manifest, permission definitions and actual call path still matter.

The sensitive sink is reply.send(body) after a raw lookup without ownership validation. The fixed variant restricts export and checks ownership, but its correctness still needs an installed build test.

Invoke a scope-approved receiver from an owned second app for own and other-account IDs; compare results and session labels. This snippet is not an installed receiver, so no delivery or leak is observed.
cases.runtime: Optional: build the separate Notes Boundary demo and compare VIEW Activity behavior; the receiver shown here is NOT part of that APK.
cases.limit: No second-app receiver test, Binder trace or permission enforcement observation exists in this pack.

cases.title: URI parsing and competing handlers
cases.fixed:
val host = uri.host ?: return
if (uri.scheme != "https" || host != "trusted.example") return
val next = uri.getQueryParameter("next") ?: return
if (!allowlistedDestination(next)) return
questions: Which crafted hostname passes the suffix check without being trusted.example?
What is separate from the URI parser check when claiming an Android App Link is verified?
What evidence would show an unsafe action actually occurred on a device?
feedback: attackertrusted.example passes the suffix comparison; so does a legitimate subdomain if that is separately authorized. Exact host matching and explicit subdomain policy are distinct decisions.
Android HTTPS App Link verification requires the installed manifest, domain association and device state; a URI host string or a custom scheme alone does not prove verified ownership.

Use an authorized test device, installed build/hash, a competing handler where relevant, controlled inputs and evidence of the privileged sink actually executing. A source trace alone is a hypothesis.
cases.runtime: Optional owned build: test Notes Boundary custom-scheme routing. It demonstrates URI entry, not HTTPS App Link verification or this fictional LinkRouter.
cases.limit: The snippet has no app association JSON, installed domain verification result or privileged sink implementation.

cases.title: Token lifecycle on a device
questions: Which two separate sinks expose token material in the vulnerable excerpt?
Does placing a symmetric key in Keystore automatically prevent an authorized app process from using or disclosing a token?
What positive/negative checks would establish logout cleanup on an owned device?
feedback: Plaintext preferences and Log.d are separate storage/logging surfaces. The excerpt alone does not prove another app can read app-private files on a current OS.
No. An app process that can request decryption can still mishandle the resulting value. Hardware backing and user authentication vary by device/key policy.
Use a synthetic test token, inspect accessible app storage and scoped logs before/after logout on an owned build, then verify session reuse fails. No real token or runtime capture is included.
cases.runtime: Requires a dedicated build and owned emulator to inspect device files/logs; this pack supports offline tracing only.
cases.limit: secureStore is pseudocode, not a shipped secure-storage implementation.

cases.title: Trust decisions versus proxy visibility
questions: What trust boundary does an empty checkServerTrusted undermine?
Is interception after a pinning bypass by itself evidence of an exploitable app vulnerability?
How do you distinguish a debug-only CA from a release-build trust decision?
feedback: Server certificate-chain acceptance is bypassed in this illustrative implementation, but hostname verification and whether this manager is installed are not shown; inspect the real built client.
No. A controlled proxy/instrumentation technique permits observation; separately test whether an unmodified release build accepts an untrusted server and what sensitive data it transmits.
Inspect merged network-security config and code for each exact build, compare controlled wrong-CA/host tests and record OS/API, certificate and client logs. No network session is provided.
cases.runtime: No endpoint, certificate chain, proxy session or APK supplied for this case; do not claim an observed TLS failure.
cases.limit: The fixed code references a third-party HTTP client only as an example; it is not a compilable fixture or dependency in the Notes Boundary demo.

cases.title: Untrusted origin to privileged bridge
cases.fixed:
val destination = Uri.parse(intent.getStringExtra("url"))
if (destination.scheme != "https" || destination.host != "owned.example") return
// Remove the bridge unless required; constrain every method separately.
web.loadUrl(destination.toString())
questions: Identify the externally controlled source and privileged sink.
Why is restricting the first URL insufficient if redirects or subresources can execute bridge-calling JavaScript?
Which device observation would distinguish arbitrary URL loading from actual bridge-method impact?
feedback: The intent extra supplies url; loading it into a JavaScript-enabled WebView with a native bridge is a high-priority review path. The Bridge implementation is absent: no sensitive action is established.
Navigation policy must be enforced across redirects and content origins; bridge exposure and origin assumptions vary with platform/API. Check bridge method annotations and loaded-content model.
On a permitted build, use benign controlled content, track final origin and bridge invocation, and document whether any sensitive action occurred. No WebView device result is bundled.
cases.runtime: The Notes Boundary app has no WebView; this is source-only and needs a distinct build for dynamic validation.
cases.limit: No Bridge method bodies, WebView client, redirect chain or browser trace is supplied.

cases.title: Dynamic hypothesis and instrumentation limits
cases.vulnerable:
Hypothesis: LinkActivity routes an external id into NoteStore.lookup.
Observation needed: invoked method + active user + returned note on an owned build.
cases.fixed:
Negative control: other-user note returns null in fixed variant.
Positive control: own note returns text in both variants.
Record build hash, device API, exact app package and lifecycle.
questions: What does a hook firing prove, and what does it not prove about account impact?
Why compare passive UI observations with an instrumented run?
How can an app restart or a debug build invalidate a claimed comparison?
feedback: A hook proves execution under that instrumented environment, not another user's actual data exposure or production exploitability. Corroborate displayed behavior and ownership on controlled mock records.
Instrumentation can alter timing, checks and trust. Pair hook observations with unmodified build behavior and repeatable positive/negative controls.
The Notes Boundary mock user resets to Alice on a new Activity instance; debug builds differ from release. Observe the account label and record artifact identity for every attempt.
cases.runtime: Owned-workstation extension uses the Notes Boundary source; no Frida scripts or measured traces ship here. Tools are optional; ordinary UI + ADB suffice for the mock lookup case.
cases.limit: An instrumentation transcript cannot be generated or graded in a browser-only course without an independently run device and trusted test harness.

cases.title: Nonce misuse and local trust
cases.vulnerable:
val iv = ByteArray(12) // same all-zero nonce reused
val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key, GCMParameterSpec(128, iv))
cases.fixed:
val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key) // provider-generated fresh IV
val iv = cipher.iv // store alongside ciphertext; never reuse with this key
questions: What relationship makes repeating a GCM nonce dangerous?
Does Keystore-backed key material by itself repair IV reuse?
What evidence separates source-level misuse from ciphertext actually produced in a release build?
feedback: Reusing a nonce with the same key in GCM destroys required uniqueness and can undermine confidentiality/integrity; the all-zero IV is a clear static misuse candidate.

No; non-exportability is separate from correct AEAD initialization and nonce management. Actual providers may reject IV reuse on encryption; verify behavior rather than claim exploitation from snippet alone.
Identify the built code path, key alias/lifecycle and generated ciphertext/IV pairs on an authorized build, with controlled test data. No key or ciphertext is shipped.
cases.runtime: No crypto app or device ciphertext is included; source-only test and a proposed owned-build validation.
cases.limit: Both excerpts are illustrative and omit decrypt, encoding, storage and key generation.

cases.title: Code loading and shipped-build scope
cases.vulnerable:
val pluginPath = intent.getStringExtra("plugin")
val loader = DexClassLoader(pluginPath, cacheDir.path, null, classLoader)
loader.loadClass("org.example.Plugin")
questions: What caller-controlled path reaches the code-loading sink?
Which missing facts block a claim of code execution?
Why can a decompiler's absence of a class fail to prove an app has no dynamic code?
feedback: The intent extra plugin flows into DexClassLoader; if reachable in a real installed build, this is a serious candidate. The file's origin/readability and execution of the loaded class are missing.
Check exported entry, actual path control, filesystem permissions, existence, signature/policy validation and whether a method is invoked. loadClass itself is not proof the payload ran.
Runtime-loaded code, reflection, native libraries, split APKs and obfuscation can hide paths from a simple decompile; inspect the exact built package and runtime evidence.
cases.runtime: No plugin file, compiled APK, JNI library or executed loader is supplied; do not claim code execution.
cases.limit: The fixed excerpt is a design alternative, not a complete supply-chain audit.

cases.title: Independent engagement decision case
cases.vulnerable:
The Notes Boundary demo source has a custom URI handler and two mock identities.
A separate storage snippet logs a token. A third WebView snippet loads an intent URL.
They are NOT one installed app or one account session.
cases.fixed:
Require a separate artifact hash/build for each claim.
For Notes Boundary, compare own ID 1 and other ID 2 in both build flavors.
Leave storage/WebView impact NOT TESTED unless a distinct scoped build exists.
questions: Which one of these claims can the buildable Notes Boundary source support as a test hypothesis?
Which two findings must be rejected as cross-fixture inventions?
What is the minimal positive/negative/retest matrix for a qualified *owned-demo* conclusion?
feedback: It supports a hypothesis that the vulnerable flavor skips local mock ownership for Bob's note when Alice is selected; runtime verification still needs compiled APK, device/API, hashes and observed labels.
A real token disclosure or WebView bridge call cannot be attributed to Notes Boundary: those snippets are independent illustrative cases and are not present in its project.

Test both flavors with own note, other note and unknown ID, record each mock user and lifecycle, inspect built manifests/hashes and repeat on an authorized owned emulator. A self-review answer is not trusted field grading.
cases.runtime: No independent reviewer, packaged APK or dynamic observations are provided by SecCraft. An optional learner build is not automatically graded or certified.
cases.limit: Do not combine independent snippets into an invented kill chain or imply this toy app provides professional engagement experience.
